newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD-Tracking Greenspan, French audit, Buba.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Tracking Greenspan, French audit, Buba.

text.p: Testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, a French audit of public finances, and the last Bundesbank meeting before a recess, will overhang markets in the coming week, analysts said on Friday.
Greenspan makes his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on monetary policy and economic conditions to the House Banking Subcommittee on Tuesday.
"He will not be too hawkish," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
"The markets will be listening to what he has to say about growth and inflation, and the interreaction between the low employment rate and wage pressures."
But Greenspan is playing a strong hand and is unlikely to upset markets, economists added.
"Greenspan can pat himself on the back -- the U.S. economy is still growing very strongly, with minimum inflationary impact," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London.
Durable goods are the only U.S. data of note over the week, economists said. The June figures will be released on Tuesday, after a previous drop of 0.6 percent.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn will give a news conference on Monday to present the results of an audit of public finances. He is also expected to announce measures planned by the government to curb the budget deficit this year.
"We are looking for measures to bring the deficit down to 3.2 percent (of GDP)," said Joanne Collins, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London.

France is expected to announce a current budget deficit of 3.6 to 3.7 percent of GDP, compared with the three percent target set out in the Maastricht Treaty for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"A deficit of 3.6 to 3.7 percent is not that much different from what we have in Germany anyway, and will increase fears of a soft monetary union," said Fishwick.
The Bundesbank will hold its last fortnightly council meeting before the August recess on Thursday.
"The mark is still going to be a very important factor," said Lifton. The mark weakened to 1.80 against the dollar in the last week.
"There is a dichotomy between economic developments in the U.S. and Germany, particularly on unemployment -- the mark could break down through the 1.80 level," Lifton added.
German money supply data will also be released next week. June M3 money supply is expected to rise 6.8 percent on an annualised basis versus the fourth quarter of 1996, according to a Reuters survey.
"The Bundesbank has not really factored in M3 for some time. Inflation is a bit of a non-issue," said Fishwick.
UK markets will digest the most influential set of data over the week, economists said, in the form of retail sales on Wednesday.
"The market will be looking at June retail sales after the huge surge in May," said Collins.
UK retail sales rose by 1.1 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in May, and by 5.3 percent year-on-year.
